questions.question: Which empirical observation about pretrained network weight distributions is most commonly reported across diverse architectures?
questions.choice_A: They are approximately zero-mean with a bell-shaped, near-Gaussian bulk but with occasional outliers.
questions.choice_B: They are uniformly distributed over fixed intervals determined at initialization.
questions.choice_C: They converge to a bimodal distribution centered at the initial weight values.
questions.choice_D: They are strictly Laplace with identical scale across all layers.

questions.question: When assessing normality of weight tensors, which approach best complements a Shapiro–Wilk test to diagnose tail behavior?
questions.choice_A: Computing only the mean and standard deviation.
questions.choice_B: Visualizing QQ plots against a normal reference and inspecting deviations in the tails.
questions.choice_C: Replacing all zeros with small random noise and retesting.
questions.choice_D: Assuming normality if the central limit theorem applies to training.

questions.question: Why is mean-centering of weight tensors often performed before quantization?
questions.choice_A: To ensure weights become sparse and compressible via run-length encoding.
questions.choice_B: To enforce symmetry so that ReLU activations remain non-negative.
questions.choice_C: To align the quantizer's zero-point with the data centroid, reducing bias and improving dynamic range usage.
questions.choice_D: To guarantee normality assumptions for subsequent calibration.

questions.question: Which phenomenon most directly challenges uniform symmetric quantization of activations?
questions.choice_A: Low variance across all channels.
questions.choice_B: Exactly zero kurtosis relative to Gaussian.
questions.choice_C: Perfectly independent channel distributions.
questions.choice_D: Heavy-tailed activation distributions with rare but very large values.

questions.question: What is a practical reason for computing per-block (e.g., per-64 or per-128 weights) statistics rather than per-tensor statistics?
questions.choice_A: Local heterogeneity in scale across parameters can be substantial, and smaller blocks better adapt scales to local variation.
questions.choice_B: Per-tensor statistics always overfit the calibration data.
questions.choice_C: Per-block statistics eliminate all quantization error for low-bit settings.
questions.choice_D: Hardware cannot support per-tensor scaling factors.

questions.question: Which normality test is particularly sensitive to deviations in the tails and is often used alongside others for weight distribution assessment?
questions.choice_A: Durbin–Watson test
questions.choice_B: Anderson–Darling test
questions.choice_C: Breusch–Pagan test
questions.choice_D: Jarque–Bera is a unit root test

questions.question: In the presence of zero-inflated activation distributions (e.g., due to ReLU), which quantizer choice is most appropriate?
questions.choice_A: A symmetric quantizer centered at the mean with no zero-point.
questions.choice_B: A companding scheme that expands small magnitudes and compresses large ones symmetrically.
questions.choice_C: An asymmetric quantizer with an explicit zero-point to preserve exact zeros and allocate more levels to the non-negative range.
questions.choice_D: A uniform quantizer calibrated to the negative tail.

questions.question: Why might small per-block sizes be preferable for post-training quantization in large language models?
questions.choice_A: They guarantee that activations become Gaussian.
questions.choice_B: They reduce the number of scaling factors and thus memory overhead.
questions.choice_C: They allow a single scale to cover all layers uniformly.
questions.choice_D: They mitigate outlier impact by isolating high-variance subsets, enabling tighter scales for the remaining blocks.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between kurtosis and heavy tails in activations?
questions.choice_A: Positive excess kurtosis indicates heavier tails than a Gaussian, which increases the risk of clipping under uniform quantization.
questions.choice_B: Kurtosis determines only the mean of the distribution.
questions.choice_C: Negative excess kurtosis is typical in ReLU activations.
questions.choice_D: Kurtosis is unaffected by outliers.

questions.question: What is the primary implication of significant inter-channel variance heterogeneity for quantizer design?
questions.choice_A: It justifies using a single global scale factor for simplicity.
questions.choice_B: It motivates per-channel or per-group scaling so each subset uses an appropriate dynamic range.
questions.choice_C: It implies that normality holds across all channels.
questions.choice_D: It necessitates switching to binary weights.

questions.question: When calibrating activation clipping thresholds for uniform quantization, which criterion directly optimizes for perceptual distributional fidelity rather than squared error?
questions.choice_A: Minimizing the variance of calibration samples.
questions.choice_B: Matching the first two moments only.
questions.choice_C: Minimizing Kullback–Leibler divergence between the original and quantized histograms.
questions.choice_D: Maximizing the number of quantization bins.

questions.question: Which observation most strongly supports the use of asymmetric quantization for activations but symmetric quantization for weights?
questions.choice_A: Weights are often strictly positive, activations are strictly negative.
questions.choice_B: Activation distributions after ReLU are non-negative and often skewed, whereas weight distributions are roughly zero-mean and more symmetric.
questions.choice_C: Both weights and activations are exactly Gaussian in practice.
questions.choice_D: Asymmetric quantization has lower hardware cost for matrix multiplications.

questions.question: How does mean-centering combined with per-block scaling affect quantization error for approximately symmetric weight distributions?
questions.choice_A: It reduces bias by aligning the quantizer around zero and reduces variance by tailoring scale to local spread.
questions.choice_B: It increases error because more scales introduce noise.
questions.choice_C: It has no effect unless the distribution is heavy-tailed.
questions.choice_D: It only helps if the mean is strictly nonzero in every block.

questions.question: Which diagnostic would most clearly reveal that weight distributions are mixtures rather than single Gaussians?
questions.choice_A: A single straight line in a normal QQ plot.
questions.choice_B: Multimodal histograms and QQ plots with curvature changes indicating different variance regimes.
questions.choice_C: Constant sample variance across all blocks.
questions.choice_D: Shapiro–Wilk p-values near 1 for large tensors.

questions.question: What is a practical drawback of using very small blocks (e.g., per-8 weights) for per-block quantization?
questions.choice_A: They force the assumption of exact normality within each block.
questions.choice_B: They necessarily increase clipping error for outliers.
questions.choice_C: They can increase metadata overhead for scales/zero-points and may degrade compute efficiency due to dequantization granularity.
questions.choice_D: They make scale estimation statistically inconsistent.

questions.question: Why might a log-domain (or power-law) quantizer be advantageous for heavy-tailed activations?
questions.choice_A: It allocates more levels near the tails and fewer near zero.
questions.choice_B: It provides uniform relative error across magnitudes, better matching multiplicative variability.
questions.choice_C: It guarantees zero quantization error for all magnitudes.
questions.choice_D: It ensures the distribution becomes normal after quantization.

questions.question: In practice, why do normality tests often reject exact normality for large weight tensors even when the Gaussian assumption seems reasonable?
questions.choice_A: Large sample sizes make tests highly sensitive, so tiny deviations (e.g., mild skew or excess kurtosis) become statistically significant.
questions.choice_B: Weights are always uniform due to initialization.
questions.choice_C: Normality tests assume independence across layers, which is false.
questions.choice_D: Gaussianity is incompatible with gradient descent.

questions.question: What calibration strategy helps manage rare but extremely large activation outliers without sacrificing too much precision for the bulk?
questions.choice_A: Setting the clip threshold at the absolute maximum observed value.
questions.choice_B: Adaptive clipping based on high quantiles (e.g., 99.9th percentile) or minimizing a loss (e.g., MSE/KL) that trades off tail clipping and bulk fidelity.
questions.choice_C: Ignoring calibration data and using initialization statistics.
questions.choice_D: Using symmetric zero-mean quantization for all layers.

questions.question: Which empirical pattern motivates per-layer or per-channel bit allocation rather than a uniform bit-width across the network?
questions.choice_A: Identical distributions across layers.
questions.choice_B: Constant signal-to-quantization-noise ratio across channels.
questions.choice_C: Layer- and channel-dependent variance and tail behavior leading to different sensitivity to quantization error.
questions.choice_D: Theoretical proofs that 4 bits always suffice.

questions.question: How do outliers in weight distributions typically affect uniform quantization if no special handling is applied?
questions.choice_A: They inflate the dynamic range, forcing a larger step size and increasing quantization error for the central mass.
questions.choice_B: They reduce the step size and improve accuracy for most weights.
questions.choice_C: They only affect the bias but not the variance of quantization error.
questions.choice_D: They are neutralized by mean-centering alone.

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes the trade-off between symmetric and asymmetric quantization for weights that are approximately zero-mean?
questions.choice_A: Asymmetric quantization always yields lower error because it uses a zero-point.
questions.choice_B: Symmetric quantization is often preferred due to simpler hardware and similar error when the mean is near zero; asymmetric is beneficial when there is notable bias.
questions.choice_C: Symmetric quantization is only valid for binary networks.
questions.choice_D: Asymmetric quantization is required whenever distributions are heavy-tailed.
